items.title: SVRF: Efficient Register Storage for Long-Vector Architectures
items.summary: Vector processors exploit data-level parallelism to provide high computational throughput, but very long vectors can make the Vector Register File (VRF) a significant source of area, energy, and register pressure. This cost is exacerbated when vector instructions operate on values with scalar semantics: although such values are architecturally represented using vector registers, they do not require full-width storage. This paper proposes the Scalarized Vector Register File (SVRF), a microarchitectural enhancement that redirects scalar-semantics vector values to a dedicated scalar register file, avoiding unnecessary allocation and access of full-width physical vector registers. The SVRF integrates with vector register renaming while preserving compatibility with the supported vector ISA. We implement and evaluate SVRF in an Register Transfer Level (RTL)-based RISC-V Vector Extension (RVV)-compliant vector processing unit supporting very long vectors. Across representative HPC and AI/ML workloads, the SVRF reduces vector-register pressure and VRF activity without degrading performance. By exploiting the resulting reduction in VRF demand, the proposed design achieves up to 15.8% VRF area reduction and up to 6% total area reduction, while reducing total power by up to 12% in evaluated configurations. Some workloads also achieve up to 1.12X speedup.

items.title: A Framework for Accelerating Transformer Inference on RISC-V for Edge AI
items.summary: This work presents a framework for accelerating transformer-based language models (LMs) on resource-constrained IoT devices. The framework targets compact LMs: BERT-Tiny (B-Ty), MobileBERT (M-Bt), MiniLM (M-Lm), Electra (E-Lt) and DeBERTa (D-Bt) -- selected for their architectural diversity and use in edge inference scenarios. The proposed flow derives lightweight instruction set extensions tailored to the non-obvious computational patterns of these models. In addition, a custom instruction is introduced to accelerate the address generation stage of batch matrix multiplication, achieving a performance improvement of 15.39--21.74% with modest ASIC overheads of 6.79% in area and 2.33% in power. To further enhance performance without incurring additional processor core hardware cost, an optional compiler-directed loop unrolling strategy is employed, trading increased code size for overall reduced execution time. Evaluation on the Synopsys trv32p3f RISC-V core demonstrates inference speedups of up to 2.19x, and FPGA implementation on the AMD Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU102 shows a 32.94% area overhead at 75 MHz, whereas the ASIC implementation using the TSMC 28 nm library incurs a 21.08% area overhead while operating at 250 MHz.

items.title: AdaptViT: Runtime-Adaptive Vision Transformer Deployment on Custom RISC-V
items.summary: Deploying Vision Transformers (ViTs) on low-power edge devices is challenging due to high computational demands. Conventional pruning frameworks require a separate compiled binary for each sparsity level, increasing storage overhead and limiting runtime adaptability. This paper presents an end-to-end deployment pipeline that transforms pretrained ViTs into a single runtime-configurable binary, enabling dynamic compute-budget switching on embedded CPUs. This is achieved by restructuring generated C kernels with modified loop bounds and binary-mask control logic, allowing execution to switch across discrete sparsity levels via compact external configuration files. Compared to multi-binary deployment, the proposed runtime-adaptive approach reduces on-device storage by up to 4.86x, requiring only 163 MB for ViT-Base instead of nearly 800 MB. To maximize pruning efficiency, we introduce a hardware-aligned block pruning strategy for Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) layers. In addition, a custom ISA extension is proposed to exploit input-reuse patterns in linear projection kernels. On a Synopsys TRV32P3FX RISC-V processor, the full system achieves up to 2.8x speedup at 65% MLP and 50% attention-head pruning for ViT-Base. The ISA extension alone provides a 1.56x speedup and 33% lower inference energy, with a 24.7% area overhead in a TSMC 28 nm implementation.

items.title: Efficient Linkage-Based Compartmentalization on CHERI
items.summary: We present an efficient linkage-based model for in-process compartmentalization built on CHERI memory safety, which enables fine-grained compartmentalization of the entire UNIX user-space, scaling to 10K+ compartments on desktop systems. The model's "push-button" compartmentalization along existing library boundaries regularly hosts 500+ compartments per process for large applications such as Chromium, far exceeding the number of concurrently available protection domains supported by other mechanisms (e.g., up to 16 for Intel MPK). Custom policies can further subdivide libraries. Of the thousands of C/C++ programs tested, only the V8 JavaScript engine required source-level adaptation (<300 lines of changed code concerning garbage collection and JIT compilation). We implement the model for CHERI-extended versions of Armv8-A and RISC-V through support in the compiler toolchain and operating system. Case studies illustrate the smooth delegation of memory between compartments, compartment-aware debugging and visualization, as well as extensibility to a complex managed language runtime, demonstrating the benefits of our single-address-space model. We evaluate using multiple processors, including Arm's superscalar Morello and, notably, the first commercial CHERI-enabled RISC-V application core---Codasip's in-order dual-issue X730.

items.title: ATLAS: A Multi-Agent Framework for Lifting Binary to Canonical Compiler IR
items.summary: Lifting stripped, heavily optimized binaries to a canonical, pre-optimization LLVM intermediate representation (IR) is essential for downstream security analysis and legacy software migration when source code is unavailable. However, aggressive compiler optimizations rewrite control and data flow, remove structural metadata, and introduce type-erased low-level idioms, causing current lifters to produce malformed or semantically divergent IR. We present ATLAS, a multi-agent framework designed to reconstruct formally valid and canonical LLVM IR from optimized disassembly.ATLAS combines (i) Structure-aware, region-level retrieval, which utilizes pseudo-probe attribution to align optimized instructions with canonical IR exemplars, and (ii) a collaborative refinement loop that closes the gap between probabilistic generation and deterministic compiler constraints. Concretely, a Lift agent generates an initial IR draft conditioned on retrieved exemplars, an Advisor agent interprets LLVM verifier/compilation diagnostics and static checks to propose localized repair actions, and a Validation agent applies the edits, re-runs toolchain verification and (when available) runtime checks, and feeds the resulting diagnostics back to the Advisor. The agents iterate until the IR is verifier-clean and behaviorally consistent, or a budget limit is reached. On HumanEval-Decompile and MBPP, ATLAS outperforms seven baselines on lifting LLVM IR, achieving 91.8% re-executability and 89.4% CFG similarity across ARM, x86-64, and RISC-V binaries. Moreover, our evaluation demonstrates that ATLAS also outperforms the Binary to C to IR pipelines in pointer-flow precision and downstream analyzability. By recovering a well-formed, machine-centric representation, ATLAS enables practical cross-ISA recompilation and verifiable binary-only migration workflows.

items.title: TALU: A Reconfigurable Tiled-ALU Grid for RISC-V
items.summary: Lane-based RISC-V vector processors exploit data parallelism well but pay a recurring cost for two common patterns: reductions, which require a separate tree pass, and deep dependent expression chains, which cannot be fused and are issued as serial vector instructions. We present TALU, a 5-stage RISC-V core whose execute stage is an NxN grid of registered ALU tiles instead of a single ALU. The grid is a reconfigurable, feed-forward spatial fabric: tiles route operands only from non-backward neighbours, and added diagonal forwarding lets a reduction collapse spatially. A minimal custom extension configures the per-tile operation, routing, and per-tile constants, and streams operands through the array. On a single fabric, TALU runs ordinary scalar code, single deep-path expressions, and multi-lane vector kernels. On the benchmark suite of the RISC-V2 vector processor, TALU is 1.8-5.5x faster than RISC-V2 and 4.5-15.5x faster than Vicuna at equal lane count, with a reduction cost (dot÷add) of 1.05x versus 1.96x and 1.26x for the vector cores. A retimed implementation places and routes at 1.03 GHz in 45 nm in 0.30 mm2, half the area of RISC-V2.

items.title: Reorienting the Vector Axis: Restructuring FlashAttention for Long-Vector Processors
items.summary: A Transformer is built around attention, whose cost grows with the square of the sequence length and dominates the layer on long sequences. FlashAttention made that cost manageable by tiling the attention matrix and updating the softmax as it goes, but almost all work since has targeted GPUs. On long-vector processors one vector register can hold up to 512 single-precision numbers. The savings of a vector instruction are proportional to how much of the register it uses, so the choice of which loop to vectorize is a first-order decision. We port PyTorch's CPU FlashAttention kernel to a RISC-V CPU with 2KB vector registers and find that it reaches 16.2% of peak floating-point throughput. The kernel walks each tile one query row at a time: the product against V is vectorized along the 64-element head dimension, the softmax's per-row maximum and sum are reductions that collapse a full register to a scalar, and the software exponential's polynomial coefficients compete with tile data for vector registers and cause spilling. We propose two techniques. The first transposes the score tile and the running output so that queries lie along the contiguous axis. The algorithm and its values are unchanged. A single parameter, the number of queries in a tile, now sets the vector length of every part of the kernel and can be matched to the machine. Both reductions also disappear. The second moves the polynomial's coefficients into scalar registers, removing the spills and cutting the softmax's vector memory instructions by 78.7%. On silicon the two together cut whole-kernel cycles by 1.84 to 2.08x at a head dimension of 64, raising floating-point utilization from 16.2% to 29.7% of peak. An FPGA of the same design ranks the changes identically and scores them higher, at 2.71x.

items.title: Execution-Time Validation of Context-Carrying Action Intents in Industrial Cyber-Physical Systems
items.summary: In industrial cells, commands from learned policies, operators and schedulers reach the controller after inference, confirmation and transport, and the plant may have changed meanwhile, for instance by an operator pause. Such a command is released, or takes effect, when it is no longer correct. We call this the execution gap and ask which component should make the last check, and against which version of which state. The Action Intent Schema (AIS) is a contract in which a producer states how long its decision stays valid and what it assumes. The runtime XAIR rechecks each intent before release, can commit its authorization atomically in the context store, and can release it as a version-conditional command, which the controller executes only if its version of the state is unchanged. In controlled ablations with declared ground truth on emulated and physical cells, OpenPLC and ARM and RISC-V boards, a check on a replica always left an unprotected interval: a pause written from a few to over 100ms after submission escaped it. Only a check in the scan of a software controller, either a controller-local interlock or the version-conditional command, closed the interval for the state that controller owns; only the version-conditional command also refused commands after a pause that had been undone. A global version revoked up to every valid command under unrelated updates. Versions scoped to what the intent reads, or to the truth of its predicates, did not; with continuous signals on the variables the intent reads, only the latter avoided false revocations, though it burdens the store as predicates accumulate. On one embedded-board core, XAIR validated 148-168 intents/s.

items.title: Stop Paying by the Letter: Accelerating Full-Chip RTL Simulation with Host-Side Tokenized Logging
items.summary: Firmware diagnostic logging (printf) is an essential debug instrument in full-chip SoC design verification, yet it imposes a heavy tax on cycle-accurate RTL simulation: formatting a 30-character, 1-argument message on a simulated CPU and serializing it through an MMIO aperture costs 3.04 to 15.23 $μ$s per call (15.27 $μ$s unweighted / 15.08 $μ$s print-weighted critical-path mean on Suite A). Unlike embedded tokenizers that target flash footprint and wire bytes with offline decoding, RTL simulation is governed by a two-regime cost function---cross-fabric SoC paths are dominated by MMIO bus stalls (84.7% of call latency) whereas local subsystem paths are dominated by on-core vsprintf formatting (61.7%)---and requires live, zero-simulation-time string reconstruction to drive UVM scoreboards. We present a host-side in-simulation tokenized logging architecture for heterogeneous multi-core SoCs that eliminates both bottlenecks with zero firmware call-site edits. Using link-time ELF format-string virtual addresses as tokens over a fixed 32-bit word-aligned slot protocol across Arm, RISC-V, and DSP cores, on-core logging collapses to a single-pass specifier scan and $(1+S)$ MMIO word writes. This removes all on-core radix conversion ($C_{\mathrm{fmt}} \to 0$), 85.0%--94.5% of deployed bus transactions, 84.6%--93.3% of MMIO bus-stall cycles, and 63.5%--90.9% of total on-core logging cycles ($2.74\times$--$11.03\times$), while a SystemVerilog monitor reconstructs bit-exact strings in zero simulated cycles ($Δt_{\mathrm{sim}} = 0$). Across 858 matched full-chip test pairs (1,716 paired runs across 1,972 runs), we achieve 100% output parity with zero simulator memory overhead, saving 1,314.85 CPU hours (-26.18%) per regression pass, cutting median test CPU time by 41.51% (Suite A) and 21.33% (Suite B), and shrinking traces by 42.84% and waveforms by 28.82%.

items.title: Agentic AI for Heterogeneous System Design Across Chip, Scale-Up, and Scale-Out Domains
items.summary: The design space of modern AI/HPC systems has expanded rapidly across compute architectures, including GPUs, dataflow processors, and RISC-V accelerators; memory tech- nologies, including HBM, GDDR, and SRAM; and interconnects such as NVLink, UALink, Infinity Fabric, InfiniBand, Slingshot, and Ultra Ethernet. No single architecture is optimal across LLM training, LLM serving, and AI-coupled HPC workloads, while the resulting combinatorial design space is too large for manual exploration. We present ArchAgent, a hierarchical multi- agent framework in which an LLM-based planner decomposes system design into chip, scale-up, and scale-out subproblems, each handled by specialist agents. A deterministic analytical evaluator closes the loop, ensuring that all performance estimates are derived from analytical models rather than generated by the LLM. On a mixed AI+HPC workload under a 1 MW power budget, ArchAgent discovers heterogeneous designs that achieve a 1.93x weighted geometric mean speedup over a homogeneous GPU baseline, while requiring only 18 evaluations compared with 100 evaluations for hill climbing, which achieves 1.65x speedup.

items.summary_zh: 论文提出 ArchAgent 分层多智能体框架，由 LLM 规划器拆分芯片、Scale-Up 和 Scale-Out 子问题并交给专用智能体处理；确定性分析评估器负责闭环评估，性能估算均由分析模型生成。
items.why_it_matters_zh: ArchAgent 将 LLM 规划与解析建模结合，可应对 AI/HPC 系统不断扩张的组合设计空间。

items.title: Minimum RISC-V: Maximum FPGA Efficiency
items.summary: RISC-V processors are now widely available for FPGAs, with most FPGA vendors replacing their proprietary soft-CPU architectures with this instruction-set architecture (ISA). Although contemporary FPGAs are increasingly resource- and feature-rich, a soft processor system---including memory---often occupies a disproportionately large footprint and delivers only modest performance relative to the potential of the target device. In this work we first design a lightweight but deeply pipelined RISC-V core that can run above 700 MHz in a mid-range device and that is capable of retiring one instruction per clock under ideal conditions. We then develop and demonstrate a new optimization method that compiles the final application binary and a specialized processor instance contemporaneously. The method expands each instruction into an application-specific encoding, removes unused datapath and decode logic during synthesis, and yields cores that remain assembler-compatible with the original program while no longer being binary-compatible with a general-purpose RISC-V. We implement example designs on RV32I (base integer), RV32M (integer multiply), and RV32F (single-precision floating-point) configurations. Our optimized RISC-V is as small as 170 ALMs and closes timing at 775 MHz in an Altera Agilex-5 device. Finally, we show that these processors can be packed into a deterministic area and stepped-and-repeated continuously without material impact on performance, enabling predictable multi-core density planning.
items.title_zh: 最小 RISC-V：最大化 FPGA 效率
items.summary_zh: 研究设计轻量且深度流水线的 RISC-V 核，目标在中端 FPGA 上运行于 700 MHz 以上，并在理想条件下每周期退休一条指令；新方法同步编译应用二进制与专用处理器实例，生成应用专用指令编码并移除闲置数据通路。
items.why_it_matters_zh: 应用与处理器协同编译为降低 FPGA 软核资源占用、提升可实现性能提供新路径。

items.title: Where the SRAM Goes: Per-Symbol Attribution of Static Memory in FreeRTOS-C and Embassy-Rust IoT Firmware on a 64 KB RISC-V Microcontroller
items.summary: Selecting a firmware stack for a memory-constrained microcontroller is usually guided by aggregate binary sizes, which report how much SRAM a build consumes but not where it goes or why. We address that gap with a per-symbol attribution method that decomposes static RAM into architectural categories - scheduler heap, network buffers and pools, task stacks, and linker-reserved regions - by bounding sized ELF symbols to the .data, .bss and .stack section ranges. The method is validated by reconciling every category sum exactly against the size-based totals for all sixteen builds. We apply it to eight cumulative firmware milestones, from a bare task scaffold to a full MQTT-over-Ethernet client, implemented twice, in FreeRTOS-C and in Embassy-Rust, on the CH32V203RBT6, a RISC-V microcontroller with 64 KB SRAM and an on-chip Ethernet MAC and PHY, with functional parity verified on hardware at every milestone. The decomposition shows that both stacks spend a nearly identical share of their RAM on networking (63.8% versus 63.9%), yet the absolute cost differs by 4.4 times: 40,719 bytes for lwIP against 9,316 bytes for smoltcp. items.title: FreeSBee: A Constant-Time Compilation Pipeline
items.summary: Constant-time execution is an important security property, especially for IoT devices, that prevents the leakage of sensitive information over timing side-channels. However, achieving constant-time execution is very hard when going down to the cycle level, at least on realistic devices. A lot of research is concerned with producing tools that either determine whether code is constant-time or that ensure it is compiled into a constant-time binary, with various degrees of accuracy. In this work, we present and evaluate a full workflow for hardening against timing side-channels during compilation. It starts with taint analysis to determine the code locations that depend on sensitive information. These are then the object of automated control-flow transformations inside the compiler to seal possible timing side-channels. We evaluate our workflow in detail on a realistic application running on a RISC-V core using both static timing analysis and statistical methods. Even though we do not reach cycle-accurate constant-time execution, our statistical results suggest that our hardened binary is safe against timing attacks.

items.title: Programmable Data Layouts via On-The-Fly Data Transformation
items.summary: The performance of modern computing systems is heavily bottlenecked by the widening gap between processing throughput and main memory latency, a problem exacerbated when an application's logical data access patterns misalign with the physical layout of data in memory. To address this, we propose a hardware-software co-design framework comprising the Data Transformation Language (DTL) and the Data Transformation Unit (DTU). DTL allows programmers to concisely express complex data layout reorganizations, which the compiler translates into efficient hardware routing configurations. The DTU, a hardware engine logically situated between the Last-Level Cache (LLC) and main memory, transparently evaluates these configurations on-the-fly to gather scattered data elements into dense, logically contiguous cache lines. By converting explicit layout transformations into virtual views, this approach eliminates the need for explicit data materialization in software. We evaluate the DTU within a quad-core RISC-V SoC using FireSim, demonstrating substantial improvements in execution speed and memory efficiency.

items.title: We Query, Therefore We Compute: On Oracle Computation beyond the Machine, with an Application to Agents
items.summary: Agentic systems use large language models (LLMs) to carry out concrete tasks. Prior work often borrows abstractions such as scheduling, caching or isolation piecemeal from operating systems, so the mechanisms it builds share little common ground, and the shared view of the two forms of agentic system, Workflows and Agents, is limited. We construct an abstract machine that provides both. We treat the LLM as an Oracle and extend a two-stack pushdown automaton with one instruction, which hands the Oracle a whole stack as its query and appends the answer to that same stack. The machine thus performs two computations, the Oracle's and a Turing-complete one that we call the Priestess. A stack that the program only appends to grows autoregressively, as an agent's context does. Two symmetry breakings, S in storage and T in transitions, make a Priestess program the operating system of the programs the Oracle runs, and produce the Agent and the Workflow as the two placements of a task's program. For internally autoregressive Oracles, the two computations synchronize at the end of every answer under certain conditions, and through that synchronization we model caching and analyse scheduling. No guarantee that holds for every Oracle can fix which content crosses between the two computations, but such a guarantee does fix the boundary itself. The construction V fits the machine to a von Neumann computer. To show that it is realizable, we propose ArchNights, an extended RISC-V ISA and a Linux-style operating system implementing the machine by design. ArchNights-SE runs on gem5 as a computer system, becomes an agentic system when it runs an LLM as the Oracle, and will be open source. Agentic systems can then be designed as computer systems are. With a foundation built and a unified view, future work can share invariants and bounds, each with its conditions.

items.title: Efficient HQC Implementations on RISC-V: A Cross-Layer Design Space Exploration
items.summary: RISC-V-based hardware/software co-design has become an established methodology for implementing post-quantum cryptography (PQC) on embedded devices. Its software programmability, extensible instruction-set architecture, and optional dedicated accelerators create a broad design space that offers the flexibility required for crypto-agility and post-deployment updates. For HQC, a PQC key-encapsulation mechanism selected for standardization, several RISC-V-based implementations have already been published. However, these works explore only a small subset of this design space. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the most comprehensive exploration of RISC-V-based HQC. Our exploration is centered around a new, parametrizable architecture framework on which we characterize 29,920 distinct architectural configurations across all three HQC security levels on FPGA. The Pareto-optimal configurations from this framework outperform the state-of-the-art RISC-V-based HQC implementation, ranging from 4.8x lower LUT utilization at 17% lower latency to 69.6x lower latency at 30% lower LUT utilization, while also requiring up to 10.6x fewer block RAMs.

items.title: RepTC: Representation-Aware Optimization for Efficient Traffic Classification on Edge IoT Devices
items.summary: Traffic classification (TC) is crucial to secure Internet of Things (IoT) networks, whose edge nodes often operate under privacy, bandwidth, and energy constraints. Yet, encrypted payloads and limited computing power make accurate, real-time TC a challenging task. Existing learning-based TC approaches often fix the input configuration a priori, even though it directly influences both predictive performance and computational cost. This paper presents RepTC, a representation-aware hardware-constrained strategy that addresses session-level TC through joint model and input optimization. The method co-optimizes network architecture, session length, and header preprocessing; this enables joint control of model complexity, input scale, and data representation within a unified resource-constrained design space. The proposed approach enforces microcontroller-class constraints on memory, model size, and computation, and yields compact models deployable on low-power edge devices. A gateway monitors traffic by aggregating sessions and either performs inference locally or offloads to a low-power edge node. Both scenarios are validated on heterogeneous embedded hardware, including a Raspberry Pi 3B+, STM32 Nucleo-F401RE, and XIAO ESP32-C3, spanning Cortex-A, Cortex-M, and RISC-V processor architectures; measured inference latency ranges from 0.63 to 18.59 ms, with MCU-side inference energy between 0.50 and 1.41 mJ per session. RepTC yields configurations that achieve high accuracy on a variety of established benchmarks: 96.21% on ISCX VPN-nonVPN, 99.62% on USTC-TFC2016, and 99.97% on Edge-IIoTset; at the same time, model size and computational requirements were reduced by up to three orders of magnitude compared with state-of-the-art methods. The results show that representation-aware optimization can improve efficiency while preserving competitive classification performance.

items.title: Morph-Aware Computing: Compiler-Ordered Updates of Program State after Topology Changes
items.summary: In wireless sensor and mesh networks, modular robots, and shape-adaptive computers, computing modules attach, detach, or are replaced while the others keep running with their local state. A value computed under the old arrangement, such as a cached next hop, stays in memory but may no longer describe the current one, so a program can send to a neighbor that has left without any runtime errors. We present morph-aware computing, a programming model in which the application specifies a corrective update of such state, called a repair, and the compiler decides when it runs. In MorphLang, the repair is a Reconfigure branch next to the ordinary branches that handle sends, receives, and sensor samples. MorphC compiles MorphLang to bare-metal RISC-V and inserts a guard before every ordinary branch, so that each module repairs its state before any other branch sees a new topology. Relying on this order, MorphC also rejects sends whose target may be a literal or a value the repair does not always refresh. For a model of the code MorphC generates, we prove in Rocq that the repair precedes every later ordinary branch for any number of roles and topology changes. This shows that send-target checking is sound for a core language. On 19 MorphLang programs derived from seven network stacks, removing the repair worsens destination validity in ten of the 13 programs that declare one and never improves it. In a reduced reproduction of a released Contiki-NG defect, a callback-based version sends to a departed parent after 60 of 384 changes and the MorphLang version after none. The guards cost 12 cycles per loop in a microbenchmark, and on an FPGA the delay from each commit to the first send to the new neighbor matches RTL simulation.

items.title: ZTA-Q: an Open-source RISC-V Platform for Accurate Quantized CNN Inference
items.summary: Low-precision inference is widely adopted in edge AI to reduce computational cost and memory footprint. However, existing open-source accelerator platforms provide limited end-to-end support for CNNs following the standard TensorFlow Lite integer inference scheme. This paper presents ZTA-Q, an open-source RISC-V-based platform that enables accurate deployment of TensorFlow Lite INT8 models. In addition to extending operator support, ZTA-Q provides a configurable post-processing datapath for studying how circuit-level approximations, including reduced multiplier precision, shared shift scaling, and simplified rounding, affect model accuracy. The proposed system is implemented on a Digilent Arty A7-100T FPGA and operates at 83.3 MHz. Evaluations on representative CNN models show that with LUT, register, and DSP overheads of 26.3%, 12.6%, and 150%, respectively, ZTA-Q limits the degradation in both top-1 and top-5 accuracy to within 0.25 percentage points.

items.title: U-Sonic: An Open-Source 8-Channel Ultrasound Transmit IP in a 130 nm RISC-V SoC
items.summary: Miniaturized ultrasound (US) probes require programmable and synchronized transmit (TX) excitation across multiple elements, while existing compact platforms often rely on limited microcontroller (MCU) pulse generators or closed-source fixed-function pulser devices. We present U-Sonic, an open-source digital US TX peripheral integrated into a 32-bit RISC-V system-on-chip (SoC). The implemented SoC integrates 8 pulser cores, while the parameterized architecture supports up to 16 channels. Each core generates single- or dual-tone bursts with programmable period, duty cycle, pulse count, polarity, and idle level, together with optional inverted stop pulses for active damping. A shared memory-mapped Open Bus Interface (OBI) enables synchronous start and stop of arbitrary channel subsets and supports composite bipolar, gated, and three-level excitation schemes. Functional correctness was verified in Verilator against a Python golden model over 4379 checked cycles across directed and randomized configurations, and confirmed on a Terasic DE10-Lite field-programmable gate array (FPGA). The design was synthesized and placed-and-routed in IHP 130 nm. The post-layout area in kilo gate equivalents (kGE), scales as 1.65 kGE plus 1.66 kGE per channel. The 8-channel instance occupies 14.9 kGE, corresponding to approximately 14.3% of the 104 kGE SoC. The register-transfer level (RTL), register descriptions, verification collateral, and software support are released as open source.

items.title: HPMicro HPM5100 RISC-V MCU integrates four 16-bit ADCs, four op-amps for analog sensing and motor control
items.summary: HPMicro has introduced the HPM5100 series, a family of 32-bit RISC-V mixed-signal MCUs, starting with the HPM5151 parts. It features a 400 MHz RISC-V processor, 416 KB SRAM, 1 MB flash, four 16-bit ADCs, four operational amplifiers, and four analog comparators. It also includes a high-speed USB 2.0 OTG interface with an integrated PHY, CAN FD, multiple UART/SPI/I2C interfaces, and 32 PWM channels for motor control. The chip supports hardware floating-point operations and DSP instructions, while the integrated analog peripherals reduce the need for external ADCs and signal-conditioning circuits. items.title: VIEWE launches 4.3-inch ESP32-S31 display development board
items.summary: VIEWE has introduced the PLCM-UES31S043H800V480C-U, a 4.3-inch smart display module that appears to be the first third-party development board powered by the new ESP32-S31 MCU. The board includes a 4.3-inch display with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.4 LE and Classic, and IEEE 802.15.4 for Zigbee and Thread. It also features USB-C and USB-A ports, a microSD card slot, RS485 and CAN interfaces, and a 20-pin GPIO expansion header with UART and I2C. The board also includes an ES8389 audio codec, two NS4150B amplifiers, two onboard microphones, four ADC buttons, a WS2812B RGB LED, and BOOT/RESET buttons. It operates on a 5V power supply and supports an operating temperature range of -20°C to +70°C. items.title: M5Stack ToughC5 weatherproof ESP32-C5 IoT controller offers dual-band Wi-Fi 6, BLE 5, and Zigbee/Thread
items.summary: M5Stack has just introduced the ToughC5, a rugged, weatherproof outdoor IoT controller built around the ESP32-C5. The device features a bright 2.0-inch capacitive touch IPS display and RS485 connectivity. The ToughC5 is an upgrade to the ESP32-base3d M5Stack TOUGH introduced in 2021, with the upgraded model featuring a more modern ESP32-C5 MCU with dual-band (2.4/5 GHz) Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5 LE, and an IEEE 802.15.4 radio for Zigbee and Thread. Other changes include faster Octal PSRAM, an upgraded RTC chip with a dedicated coin cell backup battery, a passive buzzer replacing the previous 1W speaker, and a custom power management system (M5PM1 + M5IOE1) replacing the AXP192 PMU. These features make it suitable for industrial field control, outdoor edge data collection, and smart building applications. items.title: Q8botOne – A palm-sized open-source quadruped robot with ESP32-C3, DYNAMIXEL smart actuators (Crowdfunding)
items.summary: ZeroWire Robotics Q8botOne is an open-source, palm-sized quadruped robot built around an ESP32-C3 MCU and ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL smart actuators. Designed with a unique wire-free architecture, the robot integrates all components onto a central printed circuit board also used as the structural chassis. The robot is roughly the size of a smartphone and can jog, jump, and carry up to twice its 250-gram weight. The main PCB uses a dedicated 6V/16A step-down converter for motor power and includes a battery management system for two 14500 Li-ion cells. For control, the kit includes a separate ESP32-C3 controller PCB with an Adafruit Mini I2C Gamepad. items.title: Microchip MTCH3380P and MTCH3240P capacitive touch controllers support up to 64 buttons with parallel sensing
items.summary: Microchip Technology has introduced the MTCH3380P and MTCH3240P, two new capacitive touch controllers that handle touch detection internally, making it easier to build display-free HMI devices with touch-sensitive buttons, sliders, and wheels. The main difference between the two controllers is the number of supported touch sensors. The MTCH3380P supports up to 38 self-capacitance or 64 mutual-capacitance keys, while the smaller MTCH3240P supports up to 24 self-capacitance or 32 mutual-capacitance keys. Both controllers use parallel sensing with 12 on-chip ADCs to improve touch response times and noise immunity. They also support touch detection through thick cover materials and when users are wearing gloves, making them suitable for home appliances, industrial control panels, EV chargers, and outdoor kiosks. Both also support IEC/UL 60730 Class B functional safety requirements. items.title: Dragonwing FWA Gen 6 Elite Platform combines 5G Advanced, NR-NTN, and tri-band Wi-Fi 8
items.summary: Unveiled at Network X 2026, the Qualcomm Dragonwing FWA Gen 6 Elite Platform combines 5G Advanced (3GPP Rel-19), NR-NTN (New Radio – Non-Terrestrial Networks) satellite communication, and tri-band Wi-Fi 8 with a 5×5 radio configuration. The new Fixed Wireless Access (FWA) solution features a Qualcomm X105 Modem-RF with 5G NR over satellite support, quad-frequency GNSS (L1, L2, L5, and L6), Qualcomm Turbo DSDA for 60% higher throughput compared to Gen 5, a quad-core CPU, an integrated 10 TOPS NPU, LPDDR4x and LPDDR5/5x, and quantum security (CNSA 2.0 compliant). It offers 500 MHz of aggregated bandwidth, 6- and 8-layer MIMO, peak download and upload speeds of 14.8 Gbps and 4.2 Gbps, respectively.
